The interpretive history of the *bnei elohim* ("sons of God") in Genesis 6 is among the strangest in biblical reception. The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish work preserved most fully in Ethiopic versions and read as scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, elaborated a tradition of fallen angels, the Watchers, who descended to corrupt humanity through forbidden teaching and miscegenation. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 may presuppose this reading. Augustine, in *City of God*, rejected the angelic interpretation in favor of the Sethite genealogy, with the sons of God identified as the godly line of Seth and the daughters of men as the line of Cain. Readers have also set the passage beside ancient Near Eastern traditions in which kings and other powerful men claimed descent from gods. The flood narrative that the chapter introduces belongs to the broader Mesopotamian tradition preserved most fully in the *Atrahasis* epic and tablet XI of the *Epic of Gilgamesh* (the Utnapishtim narrative), where close parallels of the flood story appear. The Hebrew word for the vessel Noah builds, *tevah* ("ark," "chest"), is used elsewhere in Scripture only for the basket in which the infant Moses is set adrift on the Nile.

Book II of the *Republic* carries two arguments that later readers have often separated. In the first, a city is built from scratch, and Socrates himself presents the construction as a way of seeing the soul at a larger scale, with the city serving as a magnified image of the person. The second lays down rules for what may be said about the gods, and here Plato was entering a quarrel already two centuries old. Homer and Hesiod were the nearest thing Greece had to scripture, and their gods lied, lusted, fought their own kin, and dispensed good and evil from two jars. The philosopher Xenophanes had mocked those portraits in the sixth century, and the Athenian jury that condemned Socrates in 399 BCE had charged him with impiety and with corrupting the young. Plato's answer is to make the founders of his city into theologians before they are lawgivers, deciding what a god must be before deciding what children may hear. In his later account, Aristotle would treat the city as natural to human beings and contest the founding premise that it remedies human neediness.

In Genesis 6 there are two things to hold: a world gone wrong all the way down, and one man who walked with God. The account of the first comes without any softening. Every imagination of the human heart is only evil continually, the earth is filled with violence, and Yahweh is sorry he made man. For Noah, the command has a concrete form: build. Reform falls outside the charge. The narrator gives more space to the ark's specifications than to the corruption that requires it, because Noah builds to a measure he did not set. The ark exists as dimensions before it exists as wood, and the only thing said about Noah's part is that he did all that God commanded him. Righteousness is named before Noah acts, and in this chapter it becomes visible as obedience, the willingness to build what a God who has seen the whole world says will be needed.

At the center of the chapter stands a sentence about God's inner life. Yahweh sees that every imagination of the human heart is only evil continually, he is sorry that he made man, and it grieves him in his heart. The grief comes before the sentence and gives it its character, since what moves the flood is a maker's sorrow over what his creatures have become. Before any rain, the first covenant in Scripture is made: I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you and your sons and your wife and your sons' wives. The promise reaches past Noah to the animals, two of every sort, and to the food that will keep them all alive. God has announced the end of all flesh, yet he also specifies, in detail, what will survive it, and the one man who found favor must gather in the creatures God is about to drown.

The city Socrates builds begins from need alone. Because no one is self-sufficient, the first citizens are a farmer, a builder, a weaver, and a shoemaker, each doing the one work his nature suits, and a city that stayed at that size would never need a soldier. Glaucon refuses to live there. He wants couches and side dishes, Socrates grants him a city with a fever, and appetite's arithmetic ends in war, because the land that fed the healthy city cannot feed the feverish one and the city must take its neighbors' land and defend its own. A class of warriors follows of necessity, and with it comes the question that occupies the rest of the reading. What kind of person can be trusted with weapons? Socrates finds the answer in a well-bred dog, gentle to those it knows and fierce to strangers, and draws from the dog the first of the city's many surprises. Because the guardian tells friend from enemy by knowledge, he is already a philosopher of a kind.

Education begins with stories, because children hear stories before they ever train their bodies. For that reason the founders must supervise the story-makers, and Socrates lays down two laws governing what may be said about the gods. God is good, and therefore the cause of good things only; for the evils of the world, which far outnumber the goods, some other cause must be found, because nothing good can harm. God does not change and does not deceive, since whatever is in the best condition is least altered from outside and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse. Out go Homer's two jars at the threshold of Zeus, every poet who blames a god for a ruined house, and every shape-shifting god of the old stories. Of all lies, gods and human beings hate most the one lodged in the soul, more than any lie spoken aloud, namely the state of being deceived about reality in the part of oneself that matters most, and a god has no such lie within and no motive to put one in anyone else.

Genesis 6 and Plato's two laws make a hard pairing. Set within Plato's accounting, Yahweh is grieved in his heart and resolves to destroy every living thing: he is moved, and he is the cause of harm. Plato's laws, though, were written against gods who do evil from caprice, and the flood has a reason. Yahweh's reason is that the earth is filled with violence, which answers part of Plato's objection and leaves the rest standing. Plato allows a god to punish if the poet can show the punishment just and the sufferer better for it, and no one is better for a flood. What he will not allow is grief, since to be grieved is to be changed. For Plato a good god cannot be touched by what is below him; for Genesis a good God is touched by what his creatures have become, and his grief measures how seriously he takes the corruption. The two builders also reach their theology at different moments. Noah builds under God's judgment from the start, to dimensions handed down by a God who has looked at the world and been wounded by it, while Socrates derives his city from human need and reaches theology only when the guardians must be educated. Both texts read inward disorder at a larger scale, Genesis moving from every imagination of the heart to an earth filled with violence and Socrates looking for justice written larger in a city. Both constructions stand unfinished when the readings break off, the ark waiting for its passengers and the city for its rulers.
